testedModels.name: Command R+
testedModels.verdict: An excellent retrieval model, but CC-BY-NC licensing rules it out of commercial serving. Not carried forward.

testedModels.name: DeepSeek V4 Flash
testedModels.notes: The closest any DeepSeek model comes to running here, and it still does not. At 284-305B parameters the smallest quantization in the usable range wants about 97 GB against 95.6 GiB of usable VRAM, so it misses by roughly a gigabyte. The one build that does fit is a one-bit quantization at 82.5 GB, which leaves too little room for a second model and takes a real quality cost to get there. This machine keeps two models resident at once by design, so a model that can only run alone is a worse fit than its size alone suggests. MIT-licensed, and available locally only through a community conversion rather than an official build.
testedModels.verdict: The near miss — its smallest usable build wants 97 GB against the 96 this machine has to give.

testedModels.name: DeepSeek V4 Pro
testedModels.notes: MIT-licensed and strong on published agentic benchmarks, so the rejection is about this machine rather than the model. At 1.6-1.7T parameters the smallest community quantization runs about 850 GB against 96 GiB of VRAM, and no lower bit depth closes a nine-fold gap. Ollama publishes it only as a hosted endpoint, which is a remote API rather than a local model and so falls outside what this machine exists to do. Recorded rather than re-tested because the answer is arithmetic, and no leaderboard movement changes a footprint.
testedModels.verdict: 1.7 trillion parameters: its smallest quantization needs about nine times this machine's memory.

testedModels.name: GLM-5.2
testedModels.notes: Top-ranked among open-weight coding models and genuinely out of reach here. At 756B parameters the smallest quantization anyone runs in practice wants roughly 239-245 GB of combined memory, and even a 1-bit build lands near 223 GB, against 96 GiB of VRAM. The only packaged option is a cloud-hosted endpoint, which is a hosted API rather than a local model and so falls outside what this machine exists to do. Recorded rather than re-tested because the answer is arithmetic: no leaderboard movement changes the footprint.
testedModels.verdict: A 756B model: the smallest usable quantization needs ~2.5x this machine's 96 GiB. Ruled out on size, not quality.

testedModels.name: GPT-OSS 120B
testedModels.notes: Measured 2026-09-05 against qwen3.6 35B-A3B on a six-task reasoning set: both answered every task correctly, so the comparison turned on cost rather than quality. GPT-OSS is the more concise of the two — 3,378 completion tokens against 15,131 — and answers a typical prompt in about 3.5 seconds. It keeps the agent tier because that tier is chosen for multi-step tool use, which this task set does not exercise.
testedModels.verdict: The agent tier: 120B of mixture-of-experts weights at 161 tok/s, and where the fleet's tool-calling work runs.

testedModels.name: Gemma4 26B
testedModels.verdict: The smaller Gemma 4 sibling. Never wired into the serving path, and redundant with the chat tier already running.

testedModels.name: Gemma4 31B
testedModels.verdict: A capable long-context generalist, tried for a day and never routed: the Qwen tiers already cover this ground.

testedModels.name: Laguna XS 2.1
testedModels.notes: The most interesting model in the sweep and the closest call. Thirty-three billion parameters with three active, a genuinely permissive licence, correct tool calling, and the fastest generation of any model measured on the coding tasks. It was not adopted because the role it would fill is already filled: the code tier went to a model that scored the same and answers in a sixth of the time. Sampled four times, it answered between seven and eight of the eight tasks correctly, failing a different one each time — which says the task set cannot separate models at this level rather than saying anything about the model. Worth revisiting when there is a role for it. Throughput measured end-to-end against the model's own endpoint on the harder eight-task set, which is a different measurement from the figures recorded in September for the models already in service — those went through the gateway on the lighter set. Compare these six candidates with each other, not against the older column: these were measured on Ollama 0.32.13 and the older figures on 0.30.11, and the engine changed a sampling default between the two, which moves a rate on its own.
testedModels.verdict: A purpose-built coding agent in twenty gigabytes, and the fastest generator tested. Held back by having no vacant role.

testedModels.name: Llama 3.3 70B
testedModels.verdict: Strong reasoning, but 74 GB is a whole warm tier's worth of room. Superseded on value for the space it takes.

testedModels.name: Muse Glimmer 30B
testedModels.notes: The efficiency result of the sweep: it answered all eight of the harder tasks correctly in the smallest footprint of anything tested, roughly a quarter of the agent tier it would have to displace, and it calls tools correctly. It was not adopted because displacing the agent tier needs evidence this evaluation cannot produce — the agent tier is chosen for multi-step tool use, and nothing here measures more than a single tool call and a single reply. Apache 2.0. A strong candidate the day that evidence exists. Throughput measured end-to-end against the model's own endpoint on the harder eight-task set, which is a different measurement from the figures recorded in September for the models already in service — those went through the gateway on the lighter set. Compare these six candidates with each other, not against the older column: these were measured on Ollama 0.32.13 and the older figures on 0.30.11, and the engine changed a sampling default between the two, which moves a rate on its own.
testedModels.verdict: Answers everything correctly in eighteen gigabytes — the smallest model here to do so. No vacant tier to put it in.

testedModels.name: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B
testedModels.notes: Generated faster than anything else tested while answering all eight tasks correctly, in twenty-five gigabytes, with correct tool calling and a permissive licence. Not adopted for the same reason as the others: the tiers it would fit are occupied, and the multi-step evidence that would justify displacing the agent tier does not exist yet. One practical trap worth recording for anyone who pulls this model: the build whose name suggests NVIDIA hardware is in fact an Apple-only build and refuses to load on this machine. The ordinary quantized build is the one that runs. Throughput measured end-to-end against the model's own endpoint on the harder eight-task set, which is a different measurement from the figures recorded in September for the models already in service — those went through the gateway on the lighter set. Compare these six candidates with each other, not against the older column: these were measured on Ollama 0.32.13 and the older figures on 0.30.11, and the engine changed a sampling default between the two, which moves a rate on its own.
testedModels.verdict: The fastest model measured on this machine, and correct on every task. Not adopted for want of a role.

testedModels.name: Qwen2.5 14B
testedModels.verdict: The quantized chat sibling: light enough to answer directly, and the chat tier's automatic fallback.

testedModels.name: Qwen2.5 14B 1M
testedModels.verdict: A one-million-token context window in 12 GB, kept warm as the chat tier. Highest request count here.

testedModels.name: Qwen2.5 32B
testedModels.notes: A general-purpose 32B kept as a middle rung between the 14B chat tier and the agent tier: 55 tok/s, correct on every task in the reasoning set.
testedModels.verdict: A mid-size general-purpose workhorse: unglamorous, routed, and still answering real requests every day.

testedModels.name: Qwen2.5 72B
testedModels.verdict: Not carried forward: a research-only licence forbids commercial serving. A licence call, not a quality one.

testedModels.name: Qwen2.5-Coder 32B
testedModels.notes: Served as the code tier for three months and was retired on measurement rather than age. It answered seven of the harder eight tasks correctly, which is respectable, but it generated at roughly a tenth the speed of its replacement while occupying fourteen more gigabytes. The decisive finding was tool calling: asked to use a tool, it writes the tool call out as ordinary message text instead of returning it in the structured field, so nothing downstream can act on it. That rules it out of agent work regardless of how well it writes code. Kept in this log because a full-precision build remains a useful reference point for what quantization costs.
testedModels.verdict: Full-precision and thorough, but the slowest model here and unable to call a tool. Replaced by Qwen3-Coder-Next.

testedModels.name: Qwen3-Coder-Next 80B-A3B
testedModels.notes: Replaces Qwen2.5-Coder 32B as the code tier, and wins on every axis that could be measured: it answered all eight of the harder tasks correctly across two runs where the model it replaces answered seven, it generates about eleven times faster, and it is fourteen gigabytes smaller. It also calls tools correctly, which the outgoing coder does not do at all — that model emits the tool call as ordinary message text, so it cannot participate in an agent loop. A mixture-of-experts design is what buys the speed: eighty billion parameters are stored but only about three billion do work on any given token. Apache 2.0, and that was read out of the shipped artifact rather than taken from a model card — 201 lines of the plain Apache text, no research or non-commercial clause. Worth doing per-model in this family: a sibling released weeks earlier carries a bespoke community licence instead, so the family name is not a licence. Throughput measured end-to-end against the model's own endpoint on the harder eight-task set, which is a different measurement from the figures recorded in September for the models already in service — those went through the gateway on the lighter set. Compare these six candidates with each other, not against the older column: these were measured on Ollama 0.32.13 and the older figures on 0.30.11, and the engine changed a sampling default between the two, which moves a rate on its own.
testedModels.verdict: The new code tier: eighty billion parameters with three active, answering eleven times faster than the outgoing model.

testedModels.name: Qwen3.6 35B-A3B
testedModels.notes: 35B total parameters with 3B active, served two ways: thinking on for interactive work, off for scheduled batch work. Measured 2026-09-05 on a six-task reasoning set, both modes answered everything correctly — and thinking cost 5.9x the output tokens to reach the same answers, turning a 2.3-second reply into a 7.8-second one. On work this size the reasoning trace is pure overhead, which is what the two modes exist to let a caller choose.
testedModels.verdict: Fastest generator here — 212 tok/s from 23 GB — and the slowest to answer, until thinking is switched off.

testedModels.name: Qwen3.8 27B
testedModels.notes: The smallest model tested and it still answered all eight of the harder tasks correctly, with working tool calling and Apache 2.0 terms. A dense model rather than a mixture of experts, which makes it slower per token than the sparse candidates but simpler to reason about. Not adopted because the general and chat tiers are already served and nothing measured here argues for replacing them. The natural first candidate if a small, permissively licensed tier is ever wanted. Throughput measured end-to-end against the model's own endpoint on the harder eight-task set, which is a different measurement from the figures recorded in September for the models already in service — those went through the gateway on the lighter set. Compare these six candidates with each other, not against the older column: these were measured on Ollama 0.32.13 and the older figures on 0.30.11, and the engine changed a sampling default between the two, which moves a rate on its own.
testedModels.verdict: Correct on every task in the smallest footprint of the whole sweep, with a fully permissive licence. No role to fill.

testedModels.name: Qwen3.8 Flash-Next 125B-A6B
testedModels.notes: Framed by its authors as an architecture preview rather than a flagship, and the smallest genuine build is 120 GB against 95.6 GiB of usable VRAM, so it does not fit at any published quantization. Its licence is the Qwen Community licence rather than the Apache terms the 27B sibling carries, which is a distinction worth keeping straight across models sharing a family name. Worth revisiting only if a substantially smaller quantization appears.
testedModels.verdict: A preview of Alibaba's next architecture, and 120 GB in its smallest real build. It does not fit.

costSaved.basis: Estimated cloud cost avoided at Claude Sonnet rates ($3/$15 per MTok); local compute free (see basisDetail)
